subject: literature
passage: For thirty-one years Haripada Sen had sorted the letters of Chandpur, and in retirement he had not lost the habit of meeting the morning mail boat. He no longer carried anything back from the landing; he simply stood at its edge while the new clerk, a young man from Comilla, counted out the bundles. Twice that winter the clerk misread a smudged address, and twice Haripada said nothing until the boat had gone, then mentioned, as if recalling an old story, a family by that name who had once lived beyond the tank. The letters reached their owners. The clerk thanked him the second time, and Haripada, embarrassed, spoke of the weather.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: A retired postmaster misses the work of carrying the mail back from the landing.
choices.B: A young clerk depends on a retired postmaster to help him sort Chandpur's mail every morning.
choices.C: A retired postmaster quietly helps his successor while avoiding seeming to correct him.
choices.D: A retired postmaster resents the young clerk who has replaced him at the landing.

explanation.why: Haripada waits until the boat has gone, then offers the right information "as if recalling an old story," so his help never looks like a correction. When thanked, he is "embarrassed" and changes the subject. The text centers on this tactful, nearly hidden help.
explanation.A: Incorrect. The text says he no longer carries anything, but it never says he misses doing so.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Haripada helps only twice and does no sorting; he "simply stood" at the landing's edge.
explanation.C: Correct. His indirect hints and his embarrassment at being thanked show help given without any air of correction.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Nothing in his behavior suggests resentment; he helps the clerk and is embarrassed by thanks.
